draft.title: First Nations soldiers
card: Over a thousand First Nations Australians served in the First World War. The true number is hard to know, because records were often incomplete.
Defence rules often barred them. The rules said recruits had to be of European descent, but recruiting officers did not always enforce them, and later changes to the rules let more men join.
Many men found fairer treatment in the army than at home. They were paid the same as other soldiers and were often judged on how they served.
After the war, much of this was lost. Many returned to the same laws and discrimination as before, and many were left out of the soldier settlement land schemes that other veterans received.
draft.remember: First Nations soldiers served despite the rules, and often met fairer treatment in uniform than they did at home.

a.q: Which statement best describes how First Nations soldiers were treated after returning to Australia?
opts: Many lost the fairer treatment they had known in the army
They were given the same land schemes as other veterans
They were treated as equals because they had served
They were banned from living in the towns they came from
a.why: Many men went back to the same laws and discrimination as before, and many were left out of soldier settlement land schemes. Equal treatment in the army did not carry over, so the idea that service made them equals is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what changed when the men took off their uniforms.

b.q: Tom, a First Nations man from Queensland, joined the army in 1916 and was paid the same as the other soldiers in his unit. Which conclusion fits this case?
opts: He met fairer treatment in the army than he had at home
He was able to enlist because no rules ever barred him
He kept his equal standing after he returned to Australia
He was one of only a handful of First Nations soldiers
b.why: Equal pay is an example of the fairer treatment many men found in the army. The rules often did bar First Nations men, so Tom's enlistment does not show that no rules existed. Over a thousand served, so he was not one of a handful.
b.clue: Equal pay in the army is a sign of how the men were treated while serving.

a.best: Many lost the fairer treatment they had known in the army

b.best: He met fairer treatment in the army than he had at home

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a qualifier ('Many'); the three wrong options are all absolute claims about 'They'. A student could pick it on that cue alone, without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The facts check out and both intended answers are right. In question a, the right option is the only hedged one ('Many'), which gives it away; rewording the distractors to match would fix this.
